For real $z>0$, let $D_z:=z^{-1}\frac{d}{dz}$ and define, for integers $\ell\ge0$,
$$j_\ell(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(\frac{\sin z}{z}\right),\qquad h_\ell^{(1)}(z):=(-z)^\ell D_z^\ell\left(-i\frac{e^{iz}}{z}\right).$$
The definition fixes the outgoing $e^{iz}$ convention. The functions solve the radial Helmholtz equation and have the recurrence, origin, Wronskian, and infinity behavior by [[lem-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-radial-solutions]].

These symbolic definitions assert no stable or certified numerical evaluation algorithm for large $\ell$ or $z$.

For the functions of [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]], define
$$L_\ell y:=y''+\frac2z y'+\left(1-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{z^2}\right)y\qquad(z>0).$$
Then $L_\ell j_\ell=L_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}=0$, and for $y=j,h^{(1)}$,
$$y_{\ell+1}(z)=\frac{\ell}{z}y_\ell(z)-y_\ell'(z),\qquad y_\ell'(z)=y_{\ell-1}(z)-\frac{\ell+1}{z}y_\ell(z)\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
The regular-origin and outgoing-infinity normalizations are
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{z^\ell}{(2\ell+1)!!}+O(z^{\ell+2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=-i(2\ell-1)!!z^{-\ell-1}(1+O(z))\quad(z\downarrow0),$$
$$j_\ell(z)=\frac{\sin(z-\ell\pi/2)}z+O(z^{-2}),\quad h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=(-i)^{\ell+1}\frac{e^{iz}}z+O(z^{-2})\quad(z\to\infty),$$
where $(-1)!!:=1$. Their Wronskian is
$$j_\ell(z)(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)-j_\ell'(z)h_\ell^{(1)}(z)=\frac{i}{z^2}.$$

derivations.claim: Direct differentiation of $h_0=-ie^{iz}/z$ gives the finite expression $h_\ell(z)=(-i)^{\ell+1}e^{iz}\sum_{m=0}^{\ell}i^m A_{\ell m}z^{-m-1},\qquad A_{\ell m}=\frac{(\ell+m)!}{m!(\ell-m)!2^m}.$ Indeed it holds at $\ell=0$; substituting this expression in $h_{\ell+1}=\ell h_\ell/z-h_\ell'$ gives $A_{\ell+1,m}=A_{\ell m}+(\ell+m)A_{\ell,m-1}$ (out-of-range coefficients are zero), and the displayed factorial formula satisfies that recurrence and the $m=0$ base.

Let $F_\ell=|h_\ell|^2$. The radial recurrence gives $h_{\ell+1}=(2\ell+1)h_\ell/z-h_{\ell-1}$. Also $F_\ell'=2\operatorname{Re}(\bar h_\ell h_{\ell-1})-2(\ell+1)F_\ell/z$ by [F2]. Expanding the squared modulus and eliminating the real cross term yields $F_{\ell+1}=F_{\ell-1}-(2\ell+1)F_\ell'/z-(2\ell+1)F_\ell/z^2.$ From $F_0=z^{-2}$ and $F_1=z^{-2}+z^{-4}$, coefficient comparison yields $S_{\ell+1,0}=S_{\ell-1,0}=1$ and, for $1\le q\le\ell$, $S_{\ell+1,q}=S_{\ell-1,q}+(2\ell+1)(2q-1)S_{\ell,q-1}$. The displayed factorial coefficients satisfy this: the ratios are $S_{\ell-1,q}/S_{\ell+1,q}=(\ell-q)(\ell-q+1)/[(\ell+q)(\ell+q+1)]$ and $S_{\ell+1,q}/S_{\ell,q-1}=(2q-1)(\ell+q)(\ell+q+1)/(2q)$, whose difference gives the recurrence. At the top index $q=\ell+1$, $S_{\ell+1,\ell+1}=(2\ell+1)^2S_{\ell,\ell}$; thus induction proves the stated sum at every degree.

Every $S_{\ell m}$ is positive, so differentiating the finite sum gives $F_\ell'(z)<0$. For $0\le m\le\ell-1$, $S_{\ell m}/S_{\ell-1,m}=(\ell+m)/(\ell-m)\ge1$, and the degree-$\ell$ sum has one additional positive term. Hence $|h_\ell|$ decreases with $z$ and $|h_{\ell-1}|\le|h_\ell|$. For $\ell\ge1$, [F2] now implies $|h_\ell'|\le|h_{\ell-1}|+(\ell+1)|h_\ell|/z\le(1+(\ell+1)/z)|h_\ell|$; for $\ell=0$ the same bound follows by differentiating $h_0=-ie^{iz}/z$.

Differentiating the finite sum in step 1.1 cancels its $ie^{iz}$ derivative in $h_\ell'-ih_\ell$, so $|z(h_\ell'-ih_\ell)|\le\sum_{m=0}^{\ell}(m+1)A_{\ell m}z^{-m-1}$. The lowest-power term of the positive modulus sum gives $|h_\ell(z_0)|\ge A_{\ell\ell}z_0^{-\ell-1}$. For $j=\ell-m$, factorial cancellation gives $\frac{A_{\ell,\ell-j}}{A_{\ell\ell}}=\frac{2^j}{j!}\prod_{s=0}^{j-1}\frac{\ell-s}{2\ell-s}\le\frac{2^j}{j!}.$ Using $z\ge z_0$ and $m+1\le\ell+1$, the quotient in the claim is at most $(\ell+1)\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}(2z_0)^j/j!\le(\ell+1)e^{2z_0}$.

Fix $a>0$, $k>0$, and $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb S^2;\mathbb C)$. Write $S_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=a\}$. The sound-soft exterior Helmholtz problem is to find a complex-valued $u\in C^2(\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>a\})$ that extends continuously to $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|\ge a\}$ and satisfies $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ for $|x|>a$, with boundary restriction $u|_{S_a}(a\omega)=f(\omega)$, and
$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\sup_{\omega\in\mathbb S^2}\left|r\bigl(\partial_r u(r\omega)-ik u(r\omega)\bigr)\right|=0.$$
The time factor is $e^{-i\omega t}$, so this is the outgoing convention. The obstacle is the closed ball $\{|x|\le a\}$; its boundary is smooth and its exterior is connected. This definition makes no claim for nonspherical obstacles or nonsmooth data.

Let $\mathcal H_\ell$ be the degree-$\ell$ spaces on $\mathbb S^2$ from [[def-three-dimensional-spherical-harmonic-space]], with surface measure of total mass $4\pi$, and let $P_\ell$ be orthogonal projection in $L^2(\mathbb S^2)$. Define $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$ by the polar-coordinate identity $\Delta=\partial_{rr}+2r^{-1}\partial_r+r^{-2}\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$. Then $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g=-\ell(\ell+1)g$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$; for all smooth $v,w$ on the sphere, $\langle v,\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}w\rangle=\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}v,w\rangle$; the spaces are mutually orthogonal and their algebraic sum is uniformly dense in $C(\mathbb S^2;\mathbb C)$. For smooth $f$, for every integer $m\ge1$ there is a constant $C_m(f)$ such that $\|P_\ell f\|_2\le C_m(f)(1+\ell)^{-m}$. For $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$,
$$\|g\|_\infty\le\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}}\,\|g\|_2.$$
For each integer $p\ge0$ there is $C_p$ independent of $\ell,g$ such that $\|g\|_{C^p(\mathbb S^2)}\le C_p(1+\ell)^{p+1/2}\|g\|_2$.
The angular Dirichlet form satisfies $-\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g,g\rangle=\ell(\ell+1)\|g\|_2^2$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$.
For every continuous $f$, the ordered partial sums $\sum_{\ell=0}^N P_\ell f$ converge to $f$ in $L^2(\mathbb S^2)$.

For real $z>0$, let $h_\ell^{(1)}$ be defined in [[def-spherical-bessel-and-hankel-functions]] and set $h_\ell^{(2)}(z)=\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(z)}$. Then both solve the degree-$\ell$ spherical radial Helmholtz equation, are linearly independent, and
$$\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(z)}(h_\ell^{(1)})'(z)\bigr)=z^{-2}.$$
In particular, neither vanishes for $z>0$, and for $k>0$, $r>0$,
$$r^2\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)}\,\partial_r h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)\bigr)=1/k.$$

Let $u$ be a classical solution of $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ for $r>a$, where $k>0$, and satisfy the outgoing condition in [[def-pe18-exterior-helmholtz-problem]]. For each $\ell$, its orthogonal projection $u_\ell(r,\cdot)$ onto $\mathcal H_\ell$ has the form $u_\ell(r,\cdot)=c_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ with a fixed vector $c_\ell\in\mathcal H_\ell$. Before imposing outgoingness, every degree-$\ell$ coefficient is a linear combination of $h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ and $h_\ell^{(2)}(kr)=\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)}$. This statement is modewise; it does not assert convergence of the partial-wave series as $r\to\infty$.

derivations.claim: By [F4], for every degree $\ell$ the projection of $u$ has the form $u_\ell(r,\cdot)=c_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ with $c_\ell$ independent of $r$. Taking the degree-$\ell$ projection of the zero trace at $r=a$ gives $0=c_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(ka)$. The nonvanishing in [F3] implies $c_\ell=0$ for every $\ell$.

Thus every harmonic projection of $u(r,\cdot)$ vanishes for each $r>a$. By the uniform density in [F2], choose for each $\varepsilon>0$ a finite sum $p$ of harmonic modes with $\|u(r,\cdot)-p\|_\infty<\varepsilon$. Orthogonality gives $\langle u,p\rangle=0$, so $\|u(r,\cdot)\|_2^2=|\langle u,u-p\rangle|\le\|u(r,\cdot)\|_2\|u(r,\cdot)-p\|_2\le\sqrt{4\pi}\varepsilon\|u(r,\cdot)\|_2$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives $u(r,\cdot)=0$ in $L^2$, and continuity makes it zero pointwise. Since $r>a$ was arbitrary, $u\equiv0$.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $|\tau_\ell|\le k+(\ell+1)/R$. The $C^p$ estimate in [F5] and the super-polynomial decay in [F2] show that for every $p$, $\sum_\ell\|\tau_\ell g_\ell\|_{C^p}<\infty$. Thus the defining series converges in every smooth norm to a smooth function $T_{k,R}g$.

For $r\ge R$, the positive coefficient formula for $|h_\ell(z)|^2$ in [F3] makes $|h_\ell(kr)/h_\ell(kR)|\le1$. The derivative estimate in [F3] bounds one radial derivative of the ratio by $k+(\ell+1)/r$ times this ratio; repeated radial derivatives are bounded by polynomials in $1+\ell$ on each compact annulus by differentiating the radial ODE in [F5]. Angular derivatives likewise contribute only polynomial factors. Thus [F2] and the evaluation bound make the extension series and its derivatives through order two uniformly convergent on $R\le r\le R_1$. Termwise differentiation is valid; each summand solves the Helmholtz equation by [F5], its trace is $g_\ell$, and its radial derivative at $R$ is $\tau_\ell g_\ell$. Summing proves the trace, derivative, and PDE claims.

For each fixed $\ell$, the finite formula in [F3] gives $r(\partial_r-ik)\bigl(h_\ell(kr)/h_\ell(kR)\bigr)\to0$. The last bound in [F3], multiplied by $\|g_\ell\|_\infty$, dominates the absolute value of this degree's radiation residual by $(\ell+1)e^{2kR}\sqrt{(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)}\|g_\ell\|_2$, a summable sequence by [F2]. Dominated convergence for this series proves uniform convergence of the full radiation residual to zero.

Let $w$ be any other classical outgoing extension of $g$. By [F4], its degree-$\ell$ projection is $d_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ for a fixed $d_\ell\in\mathcal H_\ell$. Its trace at $R$ is $g_\ell$, so $d_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kR)=g_\ell$. Nonvanishing in [F3] forces $d_\ell=g_\ell/h_\ell^{(1)}(kR)$, the same coefficient as the constructed extension in [F1]. Their difference has every harmonic projection zero and is continuous; density in [F2] implies the difference vanishes. This proves uniqueness and the well-definedness claimed in [F1].

Let $k>0$, $x\in\mathbb R$ be the Cartesian normal coordinate, and $y\in\mathbb R^2$ the tangential coordinate. Let $\sigma$ be nonnegative, continuous, piecewise $C^1$, and zero for $x\le0$. Define
$$S(x)=\int_0^x\sigma(t)\,dt,\qquad X(x)=x+iS(x),\qquad s(x)=X'(x)=1+i\sigma(x).$$
The pulled-back constant-coefficient Helmholtz operator in the layer is
$$\frac1{s(x)}\partial_x\left(\frac1{s(x)}\partial_x\right)+\Delta_y+k^2.$$
This definition concerns the homogeneous Cartesian branch only; it makes no claim for heterogeneous media, curved stretches, grazing or evanescent uniform attenuation, discretizations, or finite-element convergence.

For $q>0$, $A\ne0$, and a finite layer $0\le x\le L$ with $S(L)>0$, let a one-dimensional mode be $u(x)=Ae^{iqX(x)}+Be^{-iqX(x)}$, with the PML stretch from [[def-pe18-cartesian-complex-stretch-pml]]. Imposing $u(L)=0$ gives the reflected amplitude at the interface
$$\frac BA=-e^{2iqX(L)},\qquad \left|\frac BA\right|=e^{-2qS(L)}.$$
This is the exact continuous one-mode error for a Dirichlet termination.

derivations.claim: Parameterize the stretched contour by the real physical coordinate $x\in[0,L]$. For a source at $x'$, set $x_<=\min(x,x')$, $x_>=\max(x,x')$, and $X_<=X(x_<)$, $X_>=X(x_>)$. The functions $y_1(X)=\sin(kX)$ and $y_2(X)=\sin(k(X_L-X))$ solve the homogeneous equation and vanish at the respective endpoints; their Wronskian in the order $y_1y_2'-y_1'y_2$ is the constant $-k\sin(kX_L)$. Thus $$G(x,x')=\frac{\sin(kX_<)\sin(k(X_L-X_>))}{k\sin(kX_L)}$$ has the endpoint conditions and solves the homogeneous equation away from $x=x'$. The real parameter orders the two sides of the contour, and the one-sided derivatives in the contour coordinate satisfy $\left.\partial_XG\right|_{x\to x'^+}-\left.\partial_XG\right|_{x\to x'^-}=-1$, as required by [A1].

At $X'=x_0=L/2$, $X_L=L+iS$, and $kL=(2m+1)\pi$, the numerator magnitude is $\cosh(kS)$ and the denominator magnitude is $k\sinh(kS)$; this follows from $\sin((m+1/2)\pi)=(-1)^m$ and $|\sin(n\pi+it)|=\sinh(t)$ for integer $n$ and $t>0$. Hence $|G(x_0,x_0)|=\coth(kS)/k$. Since $\sinh t\sim t$ and $\cosh t\to1$ as $t\downarrow0$, this is asymptotic to $1/(k^2S)$. At $S=0$, $\sin(kL)=0$ and $\sin(kx)$ satisfies both homogeneous Dirichlet conditions, proving resonance. The same damping parameter in [F2] gives round-trip reflected amplitude $e^{-2kS}\to1$, so the growing cavity response accompanies vanishing attenuation.
